title: Manila War Ruins
description: Artist Name: FERNANDO CUETO AMORSOLO | Artwork Title: Manila War Ruins | Lot Info: (Filipino, 1892-1972) | Manila War Ruins signed, inscribed, and dated 'F. Amorsolo Manila 1945' (lower right) oil on canvas board 13 x 17 1/16 in. (33.1 x 43.5 cm) framed 18 1/2 x 22 5/8 in. (47.0 x 57.6 cm)
provenance: The collection of Right Reverend Norman Spencer Vincent Binsted (acquired directly from the artist). | | Literature | Sylvia Amorsolo Lazo, Amorsolo: Love & Passion, vol. II (Quezon City, Philippines: Fernando C. Amorsolo Art Foundation, Inc., 2018), ill. p. 95. | | N.B. | Fernando Amorsolo was born in Manila and began painting in his early teens, when he apprenticed to his uncle, the painter Fabián de la Rosa. He won his first prize for his paintings in 1908, and by 1914 had graduated from both the Art School of the Liceo de Manila and the School of Fine Arts at the University of the Philippines. Amorsolo's first job out of university was as a chief artist for the Bureau of Public Works and an instructor at the University of Philippines, where he would teach on-and-off for 38 years. By the 1930s he had established his own studio in Manila and was experiencing success both in and beyond the Philippines. Amorsolo was the first artist to be recognized as the National Artist of the Philippines, and his work and legacy remain "significant not only in the development of Philippine art but also in the formation of Filipino notions of self and identity" (Tim Hallman, Pioneers of Philippine Art: Luna, Amorsolo, Sóbel (San Francisco: Asian Art Museum, 2006), p.2). | | The present work depicts a landscape from the 1944-45 Battle of Manila between American, Filipino, and Japanese forces in WWII. This battle took the lives of hundreds of thousands of soldiers and civilians and ravaged historic Manila. It is now considered one of the most devastating periods of urban warfare in history, having seen not only immense human loss, but also immense cultural, structural, and urban loss. Much of the fighting and atrocities took place in and among the city, resulting in the destruction of many of Manila's most significant cultural and architectural landmarks. Manila became one of the most devastated capital cities of WWII. | | Amorsolo was witness to the catastrophic tragedy of the Battle of Manila from his Manila studio. He sketched and painted multiple scenes of the destruction throughout the 1940s, often juxtaposing the beauty of the landscape with the horror of the war. Some of these works depict vivid moments of terror and suffering, such the burning of the city or attacks by Japanese soldiers; others confront the devastation from the perspective of its impact, taking as their subject the sense of loss hovering over the landscape long after the occupation had ended. The present work is a sensitive and poignant depiction of a ruined building illuminated in a stormy glow, evoking one of Amorsolo's nicknames as "Painter of Philippine Sunlight". The ominous clouds in the background, only just beginning to erode the sunlight struggling through, create a highly atmospheric and apocalyptic scene. This work is a fascinating combination of one of Amorsolo's pre-War subjects- a light-filled, intimate landscape - and his post-War subjects - the devastating effects of WWII on the landscape and people of Manila. The placid stillness of the scene forms a haunting juxtaposition with the historical setting of the work. The beginnings of a pastoral landscape remain here, but the subject is clearly not a centuries-old façade that has naturally weathered with time. Although bright green grass and pink flowers blanket the ground, the crumbling façade, distant cityscape, and approaching storm clouds hint at the work's deeper significance as a piece of cultural and national memory.

He illustrated over 30 classics including "The Velveteen Rabbit", "The Wizard of Oz", "Mother Goose's Nursery Rhymes", "The Tale of Peter Rabbit and Other Stories", and the brothers Grimm "Fairy Tales", among many others. Before his death, Atkinson was about to publish his first book; "Jack in the Green". The story stresses the importance of kindness and the consequences of greed, a message that still holds significance today.

She graduated from Carnegie-Mellon University, Pennsylvania with her BA in drawing and went on to live abroad traveling extensively throughout Europe. Her study of the old master etchings of Rembrandt, Durer and Van Eyck among others can be found within her unique style of drawing which relies on Lipton's close attention to detail and use of fine lines of cross hatching to slowly build up form. Taking inspiration from artist Diane Arbus, Lipton chooses to work mainly in pencil causing her palette to remain in various shades of black and white which evoke the feeling of memory or photograph. Since 2011, Lipton has settled in Los Angeles, her works have been exhibited internationally and are held in numerous private and public collections.

Born in the Trastévere district of Rome in 1931, Mariani was faced with the ephemeral reality of life early on as his older brother suffered from a fatal case of meningitis. Themes of immortality and the frailty of human existence is explored throughout Mariani's work. Mariani received his formal artistic education from the Academy of Fine Arts in Rome during the 1950s, where he developed an affinity for Renaissance and neoclassical masters such as Titian and Rubens. Mariani went on to continue his academic pursuits, steeping himself within the history and mythologies of Rome and Greece from antiquity to today. Mariani incorporated the influence of many artistic and literary figures throughout history, including Anton Raphael Mengs, Angelica Kauffmann, and the Brontë sisters. Bringing themes and iconography from history to our contemporary eyes, Mariani's compositions call us to consider the many developments spanning the history of art and culture, offering contemporary audiences an alternative to mass-produced imagery of the 20th & 21st centuries. | | In 1993 Mariani settled in New York where he lived and worked until his passing in 2021. Throughout his career, Mariani received widespread recognition and exhibited in some of the world's most prestigious international galleries and institutions, including the Hirshhorn Museum & Sculpture Garden Washington, D.C.; Museum of Modern Art, New York; San Francisco Museum of Modern Art; GNAM Roma; Palazzo delle Esposizioni Roma; Palais des Beaux Art, Charleroi; Biennale di Venezia; Art Center Moscow and Leningrad; and the Philadelphia Museum of Art. | | Three Elements (Earth Water Air) epitomizes the ways in which Mariani employs the iconography of classical art to comment on our contemporary experiences. Three nudes wearing the sculptural masks of classical females run in terror as three planes of red Legos come hurtling down at them. Similar contemporary, often plastic objects appear throughout Mariani's work as allegories for pollution, environmental harm and mass production. The title of the present work, paired with the imagery of invasion, suggest a narrative of the history of human production and innovation at the cost of our environment.

This too can be said for the works of Casdin-Silver, who is also presenting more truthful depictions of women as they age to provide a counter to our contemporary aesthetics of beauty.

provenance: The collection of Norman & Myrna Katz. | | Exhibited | MIT List Visual Arts Center, Cambridge, MA, A Unique American Vision: Paintings by Gregory Gillespie, October 8, 1999 - January 2, 2000. (have Claire pull catalogue: https://search.worldcat.org/title/40990280) | | Fogg Art Museum, Cambridge, MA, Life as Art: Paintings by Gregory Gillespie and Frances Cohen Gillespie, December 6, 2003 - March 28, 2004 (have Claire pull catalogue: https://search.worldcat.org/title/52937511) | | William Baczek Fine Arts, Northampton, MA, Masters of Realism, May 1 – June 15, 2024. | | N.B. | Gillespie grew up in a Catholic family in New Jersey, and received his BFA in artistic education at Copper Union, New York. He went on to complete his MFA at the San Francisco Art Institute in 1962 after which he was awarded the Chester Dale Fellowship to continue his studies at the American Academy in Rome until 1970. Gillespie was an ardent admirer of the Dutch and Italian masters, and this time in Rome served as crucial inspiration for his later work. He returned to the US in 1971 and settled in Northampton, Massachusetts, where he began working with the group of artists known today as the Valley Realists which included artists Scott Prior, Jane Lund, Robin Freedenfeld, and Randall Deihl. In its beginning stages, Gillespie and his brother Frances Cohen Gillespie were considered the leading members of the group, but soon other members began to carve out their own niches. Gillespie's own oeuvre was consistently rooted in realism but always defied stylistic boundaries, incorporating surreal, allegorical, and even abstract forms. It was these qualities which drew in Norman & Myrna to Gillespie's work and introduced them to the artists of the Valley Realist School. | | Self Portrait at 57 is part of a larger series of self-portraits which Gillespie produced throughout his career. Some of these works place the artist within his studio surrounded by props and artist materials while others - such as the present work - depict the painter on a flat background, forcing the viewer's gaze to fixate on every detail of the figure. These works almost appear to be more of a visual record marking age, change, and growth instead of an attempt to associate the figure with his craft as Gillespie's studio portraits do. Honest depictions of age can be found through out the Katz collection, as in Harriet Casdin-Silver's 2007 self portrait titled 80+1. | | Gillespie's works are today held in corporate, private, and institutional collections across the country, notably in the Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden, Washington DC; Whitney Museum of American Art, New York; Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York; Museum of Fine Arts, Boston; and the Virginia Museum of Fine Art, Richmond.

Scott Hess was born in Baltimore in 1955. He received his BFA from the University of Wisconsin and then went on to study under Rudolf Hausner, one of the founders of Fantastic Realism, at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna from 1979 until 1984. After this period Hess settled in Los Angeles where he continues today to further push the boundaries of realism, employing old master techniques to explore conceptual narratives and the human condition within his work. As the Valley Realist group was working in Western Massachusetts during the 1970s in response to the period's shift towards abstraction and deconstruction, Hess had been working in his own way to establish the genre in Los Angeles. Although these artists stretched across the country, and were all working toward individual artistic goals, their works have garnered global attention and have collectively carved out a place for realism within the formalism and abstraction that is often ubiquitous among contemporary painting. | | Hess has participated in over 100 solo and group exhibitions internationally and has been the recipient of many awards including a Theodor Koerner Award and a Western States Art Federation Award. His work can be seen in the collections of the LA County Museum of Art, Orange County Museum of Art, Long Beach Museum of Art, San Jose Museum of Art, and the Smithsonian Institute among many others. | | The present work is part of a larger series and exhibition titled 'The Hours of the Day', which Hess based on Renaissance Books of Hours. Books of Hours were small, usually private prayer books meant to foster personal reflection and keep records of feast days, saints' days, and other important dates in the Christian calendar. Hess takes this concept into contemporary life, producing 24 works representing the 24 hours of the day. These works explore the passing of time through themes of love, desire, beauty, relationships and mortality. The Pissing Boy marks 3pm in this cycle of works, and deals with the theme of fatherhood, as a father rushes to prevent his son from public humiliation in the pool locker room but arrives too late

provenance: The collection of Norman & Myrna Katz. | | Literature | The Massachusetts Review, Paintings by Jane Lund, vol. 18, issue 1, 1975. | | Exhibited | Forum Gallery, New York, NY, Jane Lund: My Work, January 28 - March 5, 2005. | | N.B. | Jane Lund was born in Queens, New York, in 1939 and has been working in pastels for over 25 years. Lund attended the Pratt Institute at Queens College and the New York School of Social Research. She has taught pastel at a number of institutions including Smith College in Northampton, MA, and her works can be found in the collections of The Art Institute of Chicago, Chicago, IL; DeCordova Museum, Lincoln, MA; DeSaisset Museum, Santa Clara, CA; the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, MA; and the Museum of Fine Arts, Springfield, MA, among others. | | Lund is a member of the Valley Realists school; she is both the only female member and the only member whose chosen medium is pastel. Lund's exceptionally detailed compositions are uncanny and surreal, capable of evoking feelings of unnerving immediacy in the viewer. Other members of the Valley Realist School, such as Gregory Gillespie, who referred to Lund as a genius, experimented with similar veins of surrealist realism. Norman & Myrna were introduced to the work of Jane Lund through their interest in Gillespie and were instantly impressed with her ability in pastel. Lund's technical mastery of pastel is evocative of 18th century pastel portraiture such as the works of Rosalba Carriera, but she takes this practice further through her incorporation of contemporary and surrealist themes. The present work stands out against Lund's oeuvre, completed in 1975, following the Civil Right Movement of the 1960s and entering into a new age of social change, the composition can be read as a depiction of the changing role of Women within our society. The central female figure dominates the page, her gaze directed at the viewer while taking on a masculine stance which exudes an air of power and intimidation.

description: Artist Name: ALEXANDER ANUFRIEV | Artwork Title: The Lovers | Lot Info: (Russian, 1940-2024) | The Lovers signed, and dated 'A.A. 82' (lower right) oil on canvas 36 x 24 in. (91.4 x 60.9 cm) framed 40 9/16 x 28 11/16 x 1 3/8 in. (103.0 x 72.8 x 3.5 cm)
provenance: The collection of Norman & Myrna Katz. | | N.B. | Anufriev believed that each person who enters this world is accompanied by a Guardian Angel, and from this belief was borne the motif that he returned to throughout his career. In the present composition, a Guardian Angel looks down upon a couple as they sit huddled closely together, watching over them, protecting them, and illuminating the encroaching darkness. | | Alexander Anufriev was born in Moscow in 1940. In 1963 he received his BFA from Grecov College of Fine Arts in Odessa. Anufriev soon moved permanently to Odessa and became a central figure in the non-conformist art movement in the Soviet Union, where artists were holding invitation-only exhibitions out of their apartments. After surviving the 1966 earthquake that leveled the capitol of Uzbekistan, Anufriev continued to create spiritually charged works which went against the secular views of the Soviet Union. He was finally granted an exit permit in 1980 and emigrated to the United States, leaving behind his body of work which he was barred from taking with him. Anufriev settled in Boston where he met his wife Anisimova, a cellist and composer from Chechnya who was finishing a music doctorate at Yale University. The two began collaborating on Anufriev's paintings, infusing her music into his angelic compositions which increasingly featured musical instruments. | | Alexander Anufriev's pieces are part of the permanent collections of the Zimmerli Art Museum at Rutgers University in New Jersey and the Rose Art Museum at Brandeis University in Massachusetts, as well as at institutions in the former Soviet Union.

provenance: A private New York collection. | | N.B. | Harriet Randall Lumis was born in 1870 in Salem, Connecticut. She showed interest in art early on, but became more focused on creating and studying art in her early 20s. Known primarily as a landscape artist, Lumis often worked en plein air to capture the New England scenery. She was deeply influenced by impressionism and even sought lessons from notable impressionist Hugh Breckenridge. | | Lumis was an active and passionate member of the New England art community. She helped to promote local artists through the Springfield Art League, and she was one of the founding members of the Academic Artists Association which supported realism in art. She held a strong belief that realism was superior to abstraction, and her work clearly shows her preference for traditional scenes. Lumis was also a member of the National Association of Women Painters and Sculptors. Later on in life, she found purpose as an art teacher and gave private lessons for the remainder of her career. Lumis died in Springfield, Massachusetts, in 1953.

provenance: Artist's Estate. | The collection of Sydney and J. Denis Glover (by decent from the artist). | | N.B. | Artist and environmentalist Doris ("Dolly") Lindo Lewis (Henriquez) divided her life between New York, Massachusetts, the Caribbean, and South Florida. Now recognized as one of the very first, if not the first, American female surrealist painter, Lewis is known for her explorations of fertility, creation, and woman's place within the natural world. Lewis was born 1909 in San Jose, Costa Rica, and later moved to Cambridge, MA, where she attended the Buckingham School, the May School, and the Museum School. Summering on Cape Cod from the mid 1920s and moving to South Yarmouth around 1934, Lewis became associated with several New York, Boston, and Cape Cod artists and writers such as Dodge MacKinght, Howard Gibbs, Harold Dunbar, and Byron Thomas. During this period, she shifted from traditional Cape-Cod landscapes to surrealism, exhibiting these works at Boston's Museum of Fine Arts and the Provincetown Art Association. In 1937, Lewis married Anglo-Jamaican Edward Henriquez in Havana, where she spent the next twelve years. The two later returned to the states, moving to Florida in 1949, where she began to explore modernism, iron sculpture, and pottery. Lewis played a courageous role in Florida's environmental affairs and was credited by Marjory Stoneman Douglas for her efforts in saving the Everglades. Doris Lindo Lewis died in 1995 at her home in West Palm Beach. Her works can be found in the permanent collections of the Boston Museum of Fine Arts, the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, Washington's National Gallery, the Provincetown Art Association and Museum, and other collections. | | Homage to Clyfford Still was completed in the 1980s and exemplifies Lewis's ability to effortlessly shift between styles. After her time experimenting with hard-edge painting, we see Lewis start to work with more fluid forms. In this composition we can see how Lewis draws inspiration from Clyfford Still through her use of his palette but her complex layering of gestural strokes sets hers apart.
